content: Superphosphate is a type of fertilizer that is produced by treating powdered phosphate rock with concentrated sulfuric acid. In the 1840s, scientists discovered that coprolites, which are fossilized animal feces, could be dissolved in sulfuric acid to create what is now known as superphosphate. In 1840, the German chemist Justus von Liebig observed that the yield of crops was directly proportional to the amount of mineral nutrients supplied to the soil through manure. He was the first to demonstrate that the phosphate of lime found in bone meal could be made more accessible to plants by treating it with sulfuric acid. Around the same time, Sir John Bennett Lawes discovered that phosphate rock could undergo a similar chemical reaction when treated with sulfuric acid, making it a viable source for producing superphosphate. In 1842, Lawes established the first factory to manufacture superphosphate in Deptford, England. The demand for superphosphate significantly increased during the second half of the 20th century, particularly due to the development of aerial topdressing in New Zealand. This innovation allowed superphosphate to be distributed efficiently and economically over vast agricultural areas. Superphosphate can also form naturally in large quantities through the action of guano, which is bird feces. Over time, this process leads to the accumulation of phosphate-rich deposits around seabird colonies. One of the most notable examples of such deposits is found on the island of Nauru in the South Pacific. Extensive mining of these phosphate deposits brought temporary economic prosperity to the island's inhabitants but caused severe environmental degradation.
